[h1]Quick Sum-Up[/h1]
[h3]In-depth analysis further down.[/h3]
[b]No AI was used to write this review.[/b]
[hr]🟩 [b]Pros[/b] 🟩

• Well-written, engaging plot, alongside a cast of memorable characters that have distinct identity, great acting, and solid development as events unfold.

• Superb combat system: it has many build choices, abilities and mechanical diversity, on top of varied enemies and unique bosses. It balances player skill and optimized loadouts very well.

• Rewarding exploration with tons of side areas, secret locations and meaningful backtracking to obtain unique items and face hidden challenges.

• Excellent boss design, with dozens of unique foes that evolve movesets as they get damaged, have special mechanics, and are a formidable challenge on the hardest setting.
[hr]🟥 [b]Cons[/b] 🟥

• The highest difficulty scales enemies way above your level randomly during battles: they become stagger-resistant HP sponges that can often two-shot you. Textbook artificial difficulty.

• Parrying is generally unrewarding until you acquire mid to late game buffs to enhance it. It’s not worth the risk unless you make a specific build around it.

• The backtracking to 100% everything can be tedious due to the high amount of slow area transitions, and lack of fast travel in many locations.
[hr]🟨 [b]Bugs / Issues[/b] 🟨

• Very rare crashes to desktop (2 in 80+ hours) in a specific area.

• Using Steam Input with a DualSense controller may cause it to work incorrectly.
[hr][h3]Content & Replay Value:[/h3]
It took me 82 hours to complete GOW:R on the hardest difficulty, taking considerable extra time to 100% everything, except the DLC because I dislike roguelites; there’s more content if you want to play that, though. Aside from NG+ which unlocks some new upgrades and items, all other content is linear; there’s no reason to replay.

[h3]Is it worth buying?[/h3]
Absolutely. GOW:R has plenty of interesting content to go through and a satisfying progression system. It’s worth buying for full price, especially for fans of the saga and third-person action enjoyers in general.

[h3]Verdict: Excellent[/h3]
A great sequel for the reboot series, that expands lore, combat mechanics and gameplay features compared to its prequel, while retaining the same feel with very few downsides.

[h1]In-Depth Analysis[/h1]
[h3]Writing & Worldbuilding[/h3]
Overall, I found the main plot to be enjoyable and beautifully narrated, with characters having plausible personalities that change over time as a reaction to the events. Coming of age is the central theme of GOW:R, alongside maturity in general. Both Kratos and his son Atreus significantly evolve their beliefs and ways during the journey; the same goes for important secondary characters, be them allies or enemies. Apart from Odin sounding more like a Cartel boss from Breaking Bad than the majestic, imposing god he should be, the main issue with GOW:R’s narration is over-exposure during specific story segments: they’re rather dull and filled with uninteresting dialogue for the most part. Luckily this is an exception, and most of the narrative flows with an appropriate balance of meaningful dialogue, cutscenes and action.

The worldbuilding is deep and crafted with care. Aside from dialogues, there’s plenty of lore documents to know more about each of the Nine Realms’ history, traditions, mythology and society both past and present. Of course, historical accuracy isn’t a concern, since there’s a fictional God of War fighting against deities of a whole different pantheon. Each location has a high level of detail, but not much in terms of environmental narration, save for a few exceptions; GOW:R’s world is interesting, complex and coherent: lore enthusiasts will have a field day with theories and speculations about its many yet-unclear mysteries.

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
You’ll explore the Nine Realms mostly on foot, the only exception being dog-powered sleds or rowboats in larger maps. Initially, you’ll be barred from visiting most of the locations, which are unlocked as you progress in the main story. Generally, there’s an alternation of linear sections with a few side areas off the main path, and large open-world sections with plenty of secrets and entirely optional sub-locations. In each Realm, there’s plenty of secrets to find, from legendary chests to unique puzzles, secret bosses, optional quests and a mountain of lore bits. 

The handy checklist included in your map keeps track, but in many cases it will be up to you to explore carefully, since nothing apart from quest-related objectives is marked on it. In many cases, you’ll have to come back later with proper equipment, skills or after specific events to be able to access multiple locations, which is a bit tedious, but worth your time in terms of rewards and additional content. Fast travel is available between static portals, which have to be backtracked to on foot, which is a bit annoying at times. Exploring every corner, ledge, pit and ruin is fundamental to get all the unique armor pieces, weapon parts, skills and crafting resources needed to upgrade Kratos and his companions’ gear to keep up with increasingly powerful enemies, especially at higher difficulties.

[h3]Combat System[/h3]
Combat plays out in third person, with fast pacing and plenty of mechanics to consider, that evolve in depth as you progress. Kratos initially has two weapons, the Axe and the Blades, each with their own skill trees that progressively unlock as you upgrade them, and a third main weapon unlocked later in the story. Atreus will be his faithful companion, with his own dedicated skill tree, acting as a support character able to shoot special arrows and split aggro in the more chaotic battles. The system has been mechanically overhauled compared to the first GOW reboot: mechanics like perfect dodges and parries, status effects, stun bars to execute enemies, and a greater variety of enemy skills and unique abilities are all welcome overhauls. 

The combat gameplay heavily depends on your build type: some players may prefer ranged attacks, while others bank it all on high risk parries and status effects, or stunning enemies quickly to execute them. There’s a great variety of options, and the game encourages you to use all weapon abilities and experimenting with them with a Labor system that upgrades weapon skills the more you use them in combat. It’s not until mid game, however, that the combat system’s full depth and versatility truly start to shine. Expect highly spectacular finishers, devastating abilities, combos, and everything else that makes the GOW series great, but improved even further compared to its predecessor. Except for parrying, which generally isn’t as useful except when used in specific builds.

[h3]Progression & Crafting[/h3]
As you defeat enemies and complete quests, you’ll gain XP to spend in upgrading your weapon skills, Kratos and his companions’ abilities, other than Runic Abilities and Relics, which act as additional skills with a cooldown. The materials you find from chests, get as quest rewards or drop from defeated enemies, particularly named ones, can be used alongside Hacksilver (currency) to upgrade Kratos’ armor pieces and weapons, granting better stats. There are many combinations between stats, unique passive abilities of each armor, skills and relics. This opens to a great class building variety not usually seen in other GOW games, in some ways similar to ARPGs. It’s a solid progression system that steadily rewards you with new set pieces, skills and interchangeable abilities to experiment with to find the best build for your playstyle.

God of War Ragnarök feels like a perfect continuation for the previous game, and a fitting end for the Norse Saga of the God of War franchise.

The story begins nearly three years after the end of the previous game, with Fimbulwinter reaching its final days, heralding the end of all the Nine Realms, Ragnarök. When Kratos and Atreus are visited by Thor and Odin, as foreshadowed in the previous game, they embark on a quest that might lead them to prevent Ragnarök. I wanted to give a few more details here, but I'd be getting into a lot of spoiler territory.

Gameplay wise, I feel it's been improved a lot from the previous game. Kratos begins the game with most of the abilities from the last one, having both the Leviathan Axe and Blades of Chaos at his disposition. There are, of course, new abilities to unlock using XP earned through battles, both for Kratos and Atreus. And just like in the previous game, you can further customize your gameplay style both with Runic Attacks, and different types of armours to enhance specific stats. Another new addition to this game is certain sections where you'll get to play as Atreus, who has his own moves and special attacks using his bow.

When it comes to level design, it's simply great. While the previous game had a limited selection of realms, in this one you get to visit all Nine Realms as part of the story, and even though Fimbulwinter is on, that doesn't mean they're all covered in snow. As the game itself puts it, each Realm experiences it differently, and some of them look stunningly beautiful; personal favourites of mine being Vanaheim and Niflheim. The open world nature of the previous game has been expanded as well, and some realms even have completely optional areas for you to explore. Speaking of exploration, you'll come across dozens of side quests, collectibles, and all that sort of optional fluff for completionists like me.

In terms of graphics, the game looks superb, I don't think I can extend this point that much; the soundtrack is also very good, and it seems they listened to my review of the previous game, as now the soundtrack is available for purchase!

Then, there's also the matter of Valhalla. Originally a DLC for the console version of the game, in this one it's included from the get-go. I won't go into a lot of detail so as not to spoil the main story of the game, since it takes place after it, but I say it's a fitting epilogue for the Norse Saga, and very worth a playthrough. Keep in mind, though, that it's somewhat different from the base game, having a sort of roguelite gameplay loop. Still very enjoyable, and if anything, it let me experiment with all the different skills and items the game has to offer, as this mode incentivizes you to switch things up in order to progress.

All in all, an excellent game in my opinion, and one I can easily recommend.

[b]God of War: Ragnarök is not just a game, it’s a masterpiece that redefines storytelling, gameplay, and emotional connection. As someone who waited for this game to release on PC with bated breath, my journey to finally play it was nothing short of a tale itself.[/b]

[h1]A Challenge to Overcome: Region-Blocking[/h1]
[b]When the release was announced, my excitement knew no bounds, until I discovered it was region-blocked for me. For many, that might have been the end of the story, but not for me. I refused to let that stop me. I went as far as to change my country just to buy this game. Yes, Ragnarök meant that much to me. However, it’s disappointing and disheartening that many loyal fans were left out due to these restrictions. Accessibility to games should be universal, and I hope developers and publishers take note of this issue in the future.[/b]

[h1]Stunning Visuals and Breathtaking Realms[/h1]
[b]From the opening sequence, it’s clear that Ragnarök is a labor of love by the developers. The visuals are stunning, even on PC, where the fidelity and optimization shine in ways that truly showcase the craft behind it. The frozen landscapes of Midgard, the fiery depths of Muspelheim, and the colorful wonders of other realms are brought to life in breathtaking detail.[/b]

[h1]A Story Full of Heart and Depth[/h1]
[b]But Ragnarök isn’t just about its visuals, it’s about heart. Kratos, the stoic warrior we’ve come to know, continues his journey of redemption, growth, and fatherhood. Atreus (Loki) evolves into a fully realized character, and their dynamic is as touching as it is turbulent. The story dives deep into themes of destiny, sacrifice, and family, delivering moments of triumph, tragedy, and reflection that few games can match.[/b]

[h1]Combat That Redefines Epic Battles[/h1]
[b]The combat system? Phenomenal. The Leviathan Axe and Blades of Chaos return with new layers of depth, but it’s the addition of new abilities, weapon upgrades, and skill trees that make battles against gods and monsters alike an adrenaline-pumping experience.
And the boss fights… oh, the boss fights! Every encounter is an event, each one challenging, cinematic, and memorable in its own right.[/b]

[h1]Was It Worth the Effort? Absolutely.[/h1]
[b]For a game I literally changed my life (and location!) to access, Ragnarök didn’t just meet my expectations—it shattered them. It’s rare to find a game that justifies such effort, but this one did. If you’re a fan of storytelling, action, or simply unforgettable gaming experiences, this is a must-play.[/b]

[h1]A Personal Thanks to the Developers[/h1]
[b]To those debating whether it’s worth the investment or effort: Trust me. It’s not just a game. It’s a journey, a revelation, and, in my case, an adventure that transcended borders.
Thank you, Santa Monica Studio, for making a game that was worth everything I went through to play it. This is gaming at its absolute best.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Epic storytelling: A narrative masterpiece with deep emotional resonance.
[*]Stunning visuals: Beautifully crafted realms with breathtaking detail.
[*]Exceptional combat mechanics: Engaging, satisfying, and challenging.
[*]Character development: Kratos and Atreus shine with growth and complexity.
[*]Incredible boss fights: Each encounter is memorable and cinematic.
[*]PC optimization: Runs smoothly and looks incredible on PC.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Region-blocking: The game is inaccessible in many countries, leaving a significant portion of fans unable to experience it. This is a frustrating limitation for a game with such a global fanbase.
[*]Demanding hardware requirements: While understandable for such a visually stunning game, lower-end PCs may struggle.
[/list]
[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]God of War: Ragnarök is not just a game, it’s an experience that stays with you long after the credits roll. Even with its few setbacks, the heart, soul, and sheer brilliance of this title make it one of the greatest gaming experiences of all time.[/b]

The story is incredible, at least for me. As a sequel, it is one of the two best ever made, and in terms of story, it takes the first place.

The gameplay quality is extremely high. SPOILER ALERT: once you get the new spear, the gameplay reaches a completely insane level.

The world feels truly alive. Nothing feels pointless or empty. I absolutely loved it, and it is significantly bigger than the first game.

SPOILER ALERT: The development of the relationship between Kratos and Atreus is amazing. After The Last of Us Part 1, this is the best character relationship development I have experienced in a game.

SPOILER ALERT: Making peace with Freya felt really good, and the sections where we play with her were insanely fun.

Thor and Odin’s designs are fantastic. They are exactly how I imagined them. They are challenging enemies, and I especially recommend playing on hard mode.

The puzzles are much better designed and no longer overly simple, which I really appreciated.

Enemy variety is excellent. There are so many different enemy types that it rarely feels repetitive.

I also liked the number of bosses. Side bosses in particular have increased a lot.

[h1]A Great Sequel, Held Back by Woke[/h1]

[h3]Introduction[/h3]

I played God of War: Ragnarök earlier this year on my PS5, spending over 90 hours to get the platinum for both the base game and the Valhalla DLC. You can check my stats and trophies here from the comments. After all those hours of gameplay, I can confidently say that Ragnarök delivers a great experience, though it has some issues that hold it back from being a masterpiece like its predecessor.

[h3]Not Just a DLC[/h3] 
 
One of the biggest criticisms people have thrown at Ragnarök is that it feels like a glorified DLC of the 2018 game, but I strongly disagree with that take. Sure, it has a similar design and gameplay structure, but that doesn’t make it a mere DLC. There’s more than enough new content, including new realms, characters, and abilities, to call it a full-fledged sequel. The combat, which was already excellent in God of War 2018, feels more refined. Plus, the new variety of enemies and more boss fights elevate the action to another level.

[h3]Expanded Gameplay and Content[/h3] 

The gameplay in Ragnarök is much more expanded compared to God of War 2018. There’s more variety in combat options, and the game offers deeper customization for your weapons, armor, and abilities, allowing players to tailor their playstyle in even more ways. Content-wise, the game also delivers far more to do, with a much richer world to explore. One major complaint about God of War 2018 was the repetitive enemy and boss fights. Thankfully, Ragnarök improves on this significantly. While there are still some repeated enemies and bosses, it happens far less often than in the previous game. One of the standout improvements in Ragnarök is the optional content. I've found them very fun to do and the same with hunting trophies once again, like the prequel. These side quests don’t feel like chores; they’re genuinely rewarding and worth doing. The post-launch Valhalla DLC is also a cool addition. While it’s much shorter than I expected and I wish there was more of it to sink into, but I can’t complain since it’s free.

[h3]The Woke Influence[/h3]

There’s an undeniable feeling that Ragnarök leans into a more woke tone. This isn’t just a personal opinion. There’s actual evidence that points to this. The developers worked with Sweet Baby Inc., a company known for inclusive storytelling, and that influence is noticeable throughout the game. Certain plotlines and character decisions feel forced, and at times, the story becomes nonsensical. While this may not bother some players, I found it detracted from the experience, making the narrative feel weaker. Replacing Cory Barlog as the main director was a huge mistake.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3210225946

[h3]Story and Narrative Issues[/h3] 

Now, let’s talk about one of the game’s major drawbacks: the narrative. The 2018 game told a tight, focused narrative centered on the relationship between Kratos and Atreus. In contrast, Ragnarök introduces a lot more characters and plotlines, which can sometimes feel overwhelming. Unfortunately, the game doesn’t spend enough time fully developing these new elements, and as a result, the story feels rushed in certain parts. Instead of the tight, emotional focus of the first game, Ragnarök tries to do too much and wraps up many plot points too quickly. Compared to the more compact, well-told story of God of War 2018, Ragnarök struggles to find the same emotional depth and coherence. This is a huge bummer since I was really hoping for a great story and narrative after the bar set by the predecessor. 

[h3]Graphics – A Missed Opportunity[/h3]  

Visually, Ragnarök is a step up from God of War 2018, but not by much. The graphics are definitely a little better, with sharper textures and improved lighting effects. However, I can't help but feel that the game’s visual potential was held back because it was also released for the PS4. If Ragnarök had been a PS5 exclusive, I think the graphics could have been way better and more impressive. By having to cater to last-gen hardware, the game wasn’t able to push the boundaries as far as it could have, which is a bit disappointing. Still, the game looked beautiful on the PS5 and I am sure it looks even better on PC.

[h3]Music – Less Memorable[/h3]  

Surprisingly, I didn’t enjoy Ragnarök’s soundtrack not even close to as I did the 2018 game's music. The composer, Bear McCreary, is the same for both, yet, the music in Ragnarök didn’t stick with me in the same way. That's because Ragnarök’s soundtrack mainly consists of redone versions of tracks from its predecessor, with not many new compositions that stand out. This lack of fresh and impactful new music made the soundtrack feel less original and less memorable. I still occasionally listen to God of War 2018’s soundtrack because it was so impactful, but I’ve never felt the urge to listen to Ragnarök’s music outside the game.

[h3]Expands, But Doesn’t Elevate[/h3]
  
Overall, I feel like there’s not much more to say about God of War Ragnarök. The game’s strengths are obvious, and they are mostly the same as in 2018. I’ve also mentioned the negatives, such as the woke elements and narrative problems. On top of that, the fact that it plays so safe and similarly to God of War 2018, is a negative for me. When a sequel feels too close to its predecessor, it loses some of its impact for me. Don't get me wrong -Ragnarök is a great game, and I highly recommend it- it just doesn’t feel like the groundbreaking game that God of War 2018 was for me.

God of War Ragnarök stands as a formidable exemplar of contemporary narrative-driven game design, and to approach it merely as a sequel would be to understate its ambition. Santa Monica Studio has not simply extended the arc of Kratos and Atreus; rather, it has constructed a thematically dense and mechanically assured continuation that interrogates legacy, fate, and the burdens of parenthood with a gravitas rarely sustained at this scale.

From the outset, one is struck by the game’s tonal confidence. Where its predecessor (2018) concerned itself with restraint and redefinition, Ragnarök expands outward—yet it does so without forfeiting the intimacy that defined the earlier work. The relationship between Kratos and Atreus remains the emotional fulcrum, but here it is subjected to greater strain. Atreus, no longer merely inquisitive, is increasingly assertive—occasionally reckless—and the resulting tension lends the narrative a credible emotional friction. Kratos, for his part, is rendered with a stoicism that feels earned rather than imposed; his evolution is subtle, expressed through hesitation as much as through action.

The writing deserves particular commendation. Dialogue is measured, often understated, and imbued with a distinctly Nordic fatalism. Characters speak not merely to advance the plot, but to reveal philosophical positions—on destiny, agency, and consequence. Even secondary figures—Freya, Mimir, and Thor among them—are afforded a degree of psychological texture that elevates them beyond archetype. Odin, in particular, is portrayed with a disarming pragmatism, eschewing bombast in favour of calculated persuasion, which proves far more unsettling.

Mechanically, the game refines rather than reinvents. Combat retains its deliberate weight, with the Leviathan Axe and Blades of Chaos offering a satisfying duality between control and aggression. The addition of new weapon dynamics and skill synergies enhances player expression without overwhelming the core system. Enemy variety is improved, though not uniformly; certain encounters verge on repetition, particularly in the mid-game segments. Nevertheless, the overall combat loop remains engaging due to its tactile feedback and strategic layering.

Exploration is markedly broadened. The Nine Realms feel more distinct, both aesthetically and structurally, with environmental storytelling deployed to commendable effect. Optional content is plentiful and, crucially, meaningful. Side quests—often framed as “Favors”—frequently rival the main narrative in emotional resonance, a testament to the studio’s commitment to holistic world-building. That said, pacing occasionally falters under the weight of its own ambition. There are moments where the narrative momentum is diluted by extended traversal or auxiliary objectives that, while well-crafted, interrupt the central urgency.

Visually, Ragnarök is exemplary. Art direction rather than raw graphical fidelity carries the experience, with each realm exhibiting a cohesive identity. Lighting, particle effects, and character animation coalesce to produce a world that feels both mythic and tangible. The absence of visible loading screens continues to be a technical achievement, preserving immersion throughout.

The score, composed by Bear McCreary, warrants special mention. It is both grand and restrained, employing leitmotifs that evolve alongside character arcs. The music does not simply accompany the action; it contextualises it, reinforcing emotional beats with precision.

If one were to levy criticism, it would centre on the game’s structural conservatism. Despite its thematic boldness, Ragnarök seldom deviates from established design conventions. Its puzzle design, while competent, rarely surprises, and certain narrative resolutions err on the side of predictability. Moreover, the sheer density of content may prove taxing for players seeking a more concise experience.

Yet these reservations do little to diminish the overall achievement. God of War Ragnarök is a work of considerable craftsmanship and narrative intelligence. It balances spectacle with introspection, delivering a story that is as concerned with the inevitability of endings as it is with the possibility of change. In doing so, it affirms the medium’s capacity for mature storytelling without sacrificing the immediacy and engagement that define interactive entertainment.

In sum, this is not merely a continuation—it is a culmination.

[i]God of War[/i] is one of my favorite games ever, so I was hyped for this. Generally [i]God of War Ragnarök[/i] continues on with everything that made the original amazing. People often bring up the fact that there are no camera cuts in these games, and it can sound like a gimmick: it isn't. The cinematic nature of the game makes it compelling and hard to put down. 

The formula evolves with Ragnarök in some cool ways. For one, puzzle design is much better in Ragnarök; new elements are introduced allowing for more complex puzzles, and generally puzzles require more thinking, instead of being mindless distractions to break up combat segments (much more so than in the previous game). [spoiler]Playing as Atreus feels unique: he's faster and is able to inflict more damage from range. The other companions you can fight with similarly add nice variety to the experience. Kratos' new weapon also allows for more interesting combat and exploration[/spoiler]. Side quests are extremely high quality in Ragnarök. Less, quickly helping a ghost floating over body, and more, helping named allies within the game complete significant missions and receiving solid rewards for your troubles.

Unfortunately I do have complaints. One of my favorite elements of the original was the grand boss fights, challenging random enemies, and specifically the post-game Valkyrie fights. [i]God of War Ragnarök[/i] does bring some stellar fights, but overall the quality was lower in this department. The enemy lock on in Ragnarök feels terrible when you're fighting more than one challenging enemy at once (they do this a lot in the post-game); aside from the lock-on, some of the controller binds aren't ideal. I understand this was developed for a DualSense controller, but many controls could be mapped better (or add new features like slow motion swap to make up for a less advanced controller). For example, lock-on is a right stick press, and sprint is left stick press, both activates Spartan rage. There have been countless times where an attack requires I sprint to dodge it, and requires I unlock the camera to sprint properly, I end up accidentally activating and wasting Spartan rage, or taking a bogus hit. An option for the camera to auto-lock on the closest enemy, or if attacks homed in on enemies a little more (so you don't end up swinging for zero damage when visually your attack clearly hit) that would be great. Similarly, the weapons each being one direction on the D-pad was super annoying. I was constantly unable to select the weapon I wanted, or accidentally changed which attack my companion was using unintentionally (maybe I just have fat fingers, but that's not only a me-issue). Dodging feels a little off sometimes as well; visually dodging an attack but still taking damage, or attack indicator showing up super early when attacks are coming from directions you can't see.

When it comes to the story, I think they did a great job, but don't nail the ending. Kratos in particular is super compelling in his personal growth. Atreus acts more irrational, in a very teenage way, that almost always feels authentic to his character. The ending comes out of nowhere, and didn't feel that grand or climactic - the final two fights were solid though. Following that moment you interact with everyone from throughout your journey in a way that feels super inorganic and rushed. 

Generally I believe Ragnarök doesn't reach the highs of its predecessor, and has a few more lows, but it's far from a bad game. In fact [i]God of War Ragnarök[/i] is still one of my favorite games I played this year, and I'm very glad it finally released on PC. Despite it being a small step back, Ragnarök is an excellent game, and continuing Kratos and Atreus' journey is 100% worth it. Although it goes without saying, don't play this without playing the first game.

[h1]Finale of the Norse saga[/h1]

God of War Ragnarök is the continuation of God of War (2018), serving as the finale to the Norse era. The game builds on what was successful in the prequel and expands on it modestly to give the sequel a fresh feel. It is a high quality product that we've come to expect from Santa Monica and PlayStation. PC port is also the ideal way to play.

[h2]Story[/h2]

We have yet another thrilling and compelling God of War story here. It picks up directly after the events of the previous game and follows the Nine Realms' journey towards Ragnarök. While it has some pacing issues compared to its predecessor, it is still a great story and a satisfying conclusion to this era of the series. If you enjoyed Part I, you'll definitely enjoy Part II as well. Kratos' son is a bigger focus here and there are story segments where we play as him.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

Gameplay in Ragnarök is almost identical to GOW (2018). It uses the same combo-based system and relies heavily on timing and runic attacks. There is a lot of depth to it and also challenge. The game is not easy, even on Normal difficulty. To beat it you will need to get a feel for the combat and can't rely on standard button mashing. During my playthrough I felt the game was unfair in some scenarios, especially when there are multiple enemies, I believe it wasn't as unfair in the prequel. You will get hit from behind a lot and in some situations you can't avoid that. It is still a fun challenge though and I refused to drop the difficulty even during the hardest fights. The main complaint I have with Ragnarök would be the changes it introduces, or rather, lack there of. At the end of the day it really is the same as the previous one, just bigger. Yes, you have a new weapon to use (which is pretty awesome), yes, you have a bit of a redesign when it comes to shields but that still doesn't make gameplay too varied. The majority of side content is the same as GOW (2018). Artifact collecting, lore, buried treasure and chests are all here. It just feels like a very safe sequel and that's fine, this is still a high quality singleplayer game, as AAA as it gets.

[h2]RPG elements[/h2]

This was the biggest feature of God of War (2018). The ability to customize Kratos' armor and weapons to build different playstyles is one of the most fun things you can do. I personally believe Ragnarök does better in this aspect, I experimented with a few different builds and they all felt unique. In the previous game there was basically one armor you would want and that was it.

[h2]PC Port[/h2]

Solid work was done by Jetpack Interactive when developing the Windows version of Ragnarök. It performs well and looks stunning. You can adjust virtually every setting to your liking and apart from minor graphical glitches, it is a perfect port. Pair that with full controller support and this is easily the best way to play.

[h2]GET IT BOY![/h2]

God of War Ragnarök is a fantastic singleplayer experience that is worth every penny. If you like AAA games with no microtransactions, no online account requirements (PSN link is no longer mandatory) and no BS then this is one of the very best PlayStation has to offer. BUY IT BOY!
